items.followUp: State the first condition for equilibrium and explain what it means.

rubric.why: Defines equilibrium by requiring both translational and rotational equilibrium.
rubric.description: Defines equilibrium as having no resultant force and no resultant torque.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for zero resultant force and 1 mark for zero resultant torque, or 2 marks for clearly stating both types of equilibrium.

rubric.why: States the second condition for equilibrium in terms of moments or torque.
rubric.description: Explains that the total clockwise torque equals the total anticlockwise torque, so the net torque is zero.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for equality of clockwise and anticlockwise torques and 1 mark for stating that the algebraic sum of torques is zero.

modelAnswer: A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force and the resultant torque acting on it are zero.
The second condition for equilibrium is that the total clockwise torque about any point equals the total anticlockwise torque about that point.
Thus, the algebraic sum of the torques acting on the body is zero.

items.followUp: Give two examples of how the study of Physics is useful in everyday life.

rubric.why: Identifies that Physics helps us understand nature and its phenomena.
rubric.description: States that Physics helps explain or understand nature and physical phenomena.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a relevant statement about understanding nature, its laws, or physical phenomena.

rubric.why: Identifies the practical importance of Physics.
rubric.description: States that Physics is useful in developing technology, engineering, or practical applications.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a relevant application or contribution of Physics.

modelAnswer: We study Physics to understand nature and explain the physical phenomena around us.
Its principles are applied in technology, engineering and everyday life.

items.followUp: A balance shows a reading of +0.2 g when empty. State its zero error and zero correction.

rubric.why: Describes the non-zero reading of an instrument when the measured quantity is actually zero.
rubric.description: Defines zero error as the reading shown by an instrument when the true measurement is zero.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing the instrument's non-zero reading at a true zero.

rubric.why: States the relationship between zero correction and zero error.
rubric.description: Defines zero correction as the negative of the zero error.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that zero correction is equal and opposite to zero error.

modelAnswer: Zero error is the reading shown by a measuring instrument when the actual value being measured is zero.
Zero correction is equal in magnitude and opposite in sign to the zero error.

items.followUp: How many significant figures are in 0.00470? Explain briefly.

rubric.why: Gives the meaning of significant figures in a measured quantity.
rubric.description: Defines significant figures as the meaningful digits in a measurement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition that refers to meaningful or significant digits in a measurement.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example and identifies its significant-figure count.
rubric.description: Gives an example such as 2.35, which has three significant figures.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid example with the correct number of significant figures.

modelAnswer: Significant figures are the meaningful digits in a measured quantity, including all certain digits and the first uncertain digit.
For example, 2.35 has three significant figures.

items.followUp: Write the first equation of motion and identify the symbols used.

rubric.why: Gives the second equation of motion for constant acceleration.
rubric.description: Writes the second equation of motion: s = ut + ½at².
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct equation, allowing equivalent algebraic forms.

rubric.why: Gives the third equation of motion for constant acceleration.
rubric.description: Writes the third equation of motion: v² = u² + 2as.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct equation, allowing equivalent notation.

modelAnswer: Second equation of motion: s = ut + ½at²
Third equation of motion: v² = u² + 2as

items.followUp: Explain why a passenger on a moving escalator has translatory motion but does not rotate.

rubric.why: Recognizes that the rider changes position as the Ferris wheel carries them along a path.
rubric.description: States that the rider moves from place to place along the Ferris wheel's circular path.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the rider's change of position or motion along the circular path.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the rider's motion from rotation of the rider's body.
rubric.description: Explains that the rider's body maintains its orientation and does not rotate about its own axis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the rider does not spin or change body orientation.

modelAnswer: A Ferris wheel carries its rider along a circular path, so the rider changes position and has translatory motion.
The rider's body maintains the same orientation and does not rotate about its own axis.

items.followUp: Define stress and strain, and state their relationship to Young's modulus.

rubric.why: Identifies the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain as Young's modulus.
rubric.description: Defines Young's modulus as tensile stress divided by tensile strain within the elastic limit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct ratio and, where included, its elastic-limit condition.

rubric.why: Gives the SI unit of Young's modulus.
rubric.description: States that the SI unit is the pascal (Pa), equivalent to N/m².
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for Pa or an equivalent SI unit.

modelAnswer: Young's modulus is the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain within the elastic limit.
Its SI unit is the pascal (Pa), or N/m².

items.followUp: State Archimedes' principle and name the force it describes.

rubric.why: Identifies upthrust as an upward force exerted by a fluid on an immersed body.
rubric.description: Defines upthrust as the upward force exerted by a fluid on a body immersed in it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the upward force and the fluid acting on the immersed body.

rubric.why: Connects the upthrust to the weight of displaced fluid, as described by Archimedes' principle.
rubric.description: States that upthrust is equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by the body.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct equality with the weight of displaced fluid.

modelAnswer: Upthrust is the upward force exerted by a fluid on a body partially or completely immersed in it.
It is equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by the body.
